source_passages.statement_original:
We consider $K$ data sources that generate data simultaneously in discrete time and denote by $X_n^k$ the random element whose value is generated by data source $k\in[K]$ at time $n\in\mathbb N$. For any subset of data sources, $s\subseteq[K]$, we set
\[
X_n^s:=\{X_n^k:k\in s\}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal F_n^s:=\sigma(X_m^s:m\in[n]),\qquad n\in\mathbb N,
\]
i.e., $X_n^s$ is the set of observations by the data sources in $s$ at time $n$ and $\mathcal F_n^s$ the $\sigma$-field generated by the observations from the data sources in $s$ up to time $n$, and
\[
X^s:=\{X_n^s,n\in\mathbb N\}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal F^s:=\sigma(\mathcal F_n^s,n\in\mathbb N),
\]
i.e., $X^s$ is the complete sequence of observations by the data sources in $s$ and $\mathcal F^s$ the $\sigma$-field it generates. In what follows, we omit the superscipt in the above notations whenever $s=[K]$, and replace it by $k$ whenever $s=\{k\}$ for some $k\in[K]$.

We consider a finite family, $\mathcal P$, of plausible distributions of $X$, to the elements of which we refer as global distributions. We say that two subsets of data sources $s_1\subseteq[K]$ and $s_2\subseteq[K]$ are independent under some $P\in\mathcal P$ if $X^{s_1}$ and $X^{s_2}$ are independent under $P$. For any global distribution, $P\in\mathcal P$, and any subset of sources, $s\subseteq[K]$, we denote by $P^s$ the restriction of $P$ on $\mathcal F^s$, i.e., the marginal distribution of $X^s$ under $P$. For any family of global distributions, $\mathcal Q\subseteq\mathcal P$, and any subset of data sources, $s\subseteq[K]$, we set
\[
\mathcal Q^s:=\{P^s:P\in\mathcal Q\},
\]
e.g., $\mathcal P^s$ is the family of distributions of $X^s$ induced by $\mathcal P$. As before, we omit the superscript whenever $s=[K]$, and replace it by $k$ whenever $s=\{k\}$ for some $k\in[K]$.

source_passages.local_label: Section 2.3 — A family of local hypotheses
source_passages.source_heading: Section 2.3 — A family of local hypotheses
source_passages.statement_original:
We consider a finite family of subsets of $[K]$, $\mathcal K$, to the elements of which we refer as units. For each $e\in\mathcal K$, we consider two hypotheses for the marginal distribution of $X^e$,
\[
\mathcal H^e\text{ (null)}\qquad\text{versus}\qquad\mathcal G^e\text{ (alternative)},
\]
where $\mathcal H^e$, $\mathcal G^e$ are non-empty, disjoint subfamilies of $\mathcal P^e$. For any global distribution, $P\in\mathcal P$, we we say that $e\in\mathcal K$ is a signal under $P$ if $P^e\in\mathcal G^e$, and we denote by $\mathcal A(P)$ the set of signals under $P$, i.e.,
\[
\mathcal A(P):=\{e\in\mathcal K:P^e\in\mathcal G^e\}.
\]

source_passages.statement_original:
We assume that the set of signals is known a priori to belong to a family of subsets of $\mathcal K$, $\Psi$, and denote by $\mathcal P_\Psi$ the family of global distributions that are compatible with $\Psi$, i.e.,
\[
\mathcal P_\Psi:=\{P\in\mathcal P:P^e\in\mathcal H^e\cup\mathcal G^e\text{ for every }e\in\mathcal K\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal A(P)\in\Psi\}.
\]
We refer to $\mathcal H_0\equiv\mathcal P_\emptyset$ as the family of global null distributions. Clearly, $\mathcal H_0\subseteq\mathcal P_\Psi\Longleftrightarrow\emptyset\in\Psi$.

source_passages.statement_original:
For example, if it is assumed that there are at least $l$ and at most $u$ signals, then $\Psi$ takes the following form:
\[
\Psi_{l,u}:=\{A\subseteq\mathcal K:l\leq|A|\leq u\}.
\]
When, in particular, $l=0$ and $u=K$, $\Psi_{l,u}$ coincides with the powerset of $\mathcal K$ and corresponds to the case of no prior information about the signals whatsoever.

naming_context.text: Throughout this subsection we assume that the data sources are independent, i.e., (21) holds, and that arbitrary lower and upper bounds, $l$ and $u$, are given on the number of signals, i.e., $\Psi=\Psi_{l,u}$.

source_passages.statement_original:
Alternatively, the available prior information may be of topological nature. For example, if the signals are assumed to form a cluster, in the sense of being stable with respect to symmetric differences, then $\Psi$ takes the following form:
\[
\Psi_{\mathrm{clus}}:=\{A\subseteq\mathcal K:\text{if }e,e'\in A\text{ and }e\triangle e'\in\mathcal K,\text{ then }e\triangle e'\in A\}.
\]

Alternatively, if the signals are assumed to be disjoint, then $\Psi$ becomes
\[
\Psi_{\mathrm{dis}}:=\{A\subseteq\mathcal K:\text{if }e,e'\in A\text{ then }e\cap e'=\emptyset\}.
\]

More formally, we say that $(T,D)$ is a test if

• $T$ is an $\{\mathcal F_n\}$-stopping time, i.e., $\{T=n\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$,

• $D$ is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable and $\Psi$-valued, i.e., $\{T=n,D=A\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$, $A\in\Psi$,

and we denote by $\mathcal C_\Psi$ the family of all tests.

When $\emptyset\notin\Psi$, false alarms and missed detection are not possible. In this case, we consider tests that control the probabilities of false positives and false negatives, as in classical familywise error control. That is, the class of tests of interest is
\[
\mathcal C_\Psi(\gamma,\delta):=\{(T,D)\in\mathcal C_\Psi:P(D\setminus\mathcal A(P)\ne\emptyset)\leq\gamma\quad\&\quad P(\mathcal A(P)\setminus D\ne\emptyset,D\ne\emptyset)\leq\delta\quad\forall P\in\mathcal P_\Psi\},
\]
where $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are user-specified tolerance levels in $(0,1)$.

naming_context.text: 2.8.1. Pure isolation.

source_passages.statement_original:
When $\emptyset\in\Psi$, or equivalently $\mathcal H_0\subseteq\mathcal P_\Psi$, false alarms and missed detections are possible. If, also, these are the only errors we want to explicitly control, the class of tests of interest becomes
\[
\mathcal D_\Psi(\alpha,\beta):=\{(T,D)\in\mathcal C_\Psi:P(D\ne\emptyset)\leq\alpha\quad\forall P\in\mathcal H_0\quad\&\quad P(D=\emptyset)\leq\beta\quad\forall P\in\mathcal P_\Psi\setminus\mathcal H_0\},
\]
where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are user-specified tolerance levels in $(0,1)$.

naming_context.text: 2.8.2. Pure detection.

source_passages.statement_original:
\[
\mathcal E_\Psi(\gamma,\delta):=\{(T,D)\in\mathcal C_\Psi:P(D\setminus\mathcal A(P)\ne\emptyset)\leq\gamma\quad\&\quad P(\mathcal A(P)\setminus D\ne\emptyset)\leq\delta\quad\forall P\in\mathcal P_\Psi\},
\]
where, as before, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are user-specified tolerance levels in $(0,1)$.

naming_context.text: 2.8.3. Familywise error control.

source_passages.statement_original:
Specifically, the proposed class of tests is
\[
\mathcal C_\Psi(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta):=\mathcal D_\Psi(\alpha,\beta)\cap\mathcal C_{\Psi\setminus\emptyset}(\gamma,\delta),
\]
where $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ are user-specified tolerance levels in $(0,1)$.

source_passages.statement_original:
In order to do so, for each unit $e\in\mathcal K$ we denote by $\mathcal H_{\Psi,e}$ the family of non-null global distributions under which the null is correct in unit $e$, and by $\mathcal G_{\Psi,e}$ the family of global distributions under which $e$ is a signal, i.e.,
\[
\mathcal H_{\Psi,e}:=\{P\in\mathcal P_\Psi\setminus\mathcal H_0:e\notin\mathcal A(P)\}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal G_{\Psi,e}:=\{P\in\mathcal P_\Psi:e\in\mathcal A(P)\}.
\]

We assume that for every
\[
e\in\mathcal K,\quad P\in\mathcal G_{\Psi,e}\cup\mathcal H_0,\quad Q\in\mathcal H_{\Psi,e}\cup\mathcal H_0,\quad e\subseteq s\subseteq[K],\quad n\in\mathbb N,
\]
$P^s$ and $Q^s$, i.e, the marginal distributions of $X^s$ under $P$ and $Q$ respectively, are mutually absolutely continuous when restricted to $\mathcal F_n^s$,

and we denote the corresponding likelihood ratio (Radon-Nikodym derivative) and log-likelihood ratio as follows:
\[
\Lambda_n(P^s,Q^s):=\frac{dP^s}{dQ^s}(\mathcal F_n^s)\quad\text{and}\quad Z_n(P^s,Q^s):=\log\Lambda_n(P^s,Q^s).
\]

\Lambda_{e,\mathrm{det}}(n):=\frac{\max\{\Lambda_n(P,P_0):P\in\mathcal G_{\Psi,e}^{s_e}\}}{\max\{\Lambda_n(P,P_0):P\in\mathcal H_0^{s_e}\}},
\]

naming_context.text: Thus, we refer to $s_e$ as the detection subsystem for unit $e$ and to $\Lambda_{e,\mathrm{det}}$ as the detection statistic for unit $e$.

source_passages.statement_original:

\]

source_passages.statement_original:
For each $n\in\mathbb N$ we also denote by $D_{\mathrm{iso}}(n)$ the set of units whose isolation statistics at time $n$ have values larger than $1$, i.e.,
\[
D_{\mathrm{iso}}(n):=\{e\in\mathcal K:\Lambda_{e,\mathrm{iso}}(n)>1\}.
\]
(4)
Therefore, $D_{\mathrm{iso}}(n)$ can be interpreted as the estimated signal set based on the from the isolation subsystems in the first $n$ time instances.

We refer to $\Lambda_e(n)$ as the local statistic of unit $e$ at time $n$, as it is computed based solely on data from unit $e$ up to time $n$. Furthermore, we denote the ordered versions of the local statistics by $\Lambda_{(1)}(n)\geq\cdots\geq\Lambda_{(|\mathcal K|)}(n)$, and the corresponding indices by $i_1(n),\ldots,i_{|\mathcal K|}(n)$. We also denote by $p(n)$ the number of units whose local statistics at time $n$ have values larger than $1$, i.e., $p(n):=|\{e\in\mathcal K:\Lambda_e(n)>1\}|$.

source_passages.statement_original:
When $\emptyset\notin\Psi$, we stop sampling when the value of every isolation statistic is either too large or too small, and we identify as signals those units for which these values are large. Therefore, the proposed test in this case, $\chi^*:=(T^*,D^*)$, is:
\[
T^*:=\inf\{n\in\mathbb N:D_{\mathrm{iso}}(n)\in\Psi,\ \Lambda_{e,\mathrm{iso}}(n)\notin(1/A_e,B_e)\ \forall e\in\mathcal K\}\quad\text{and}\quad D^*:=D_{\mathrm{iso}}(T^*),
\]
where $\{A_e,B_e\}_{e\in\mathcal K}$ are thresholds to be determined so that $\chi^*\in\mathcal C_\Psi(\gamma,\delta)$.

source_passages.local_label: Section 3.2.2 — The test for pure detection
source_passages.source_heading: Section 3.2.2 — The test for pure detection
source_passages.statement_original:
When $\emptyset\in\Psi$ and the focus is on the pure detection problem, we stop sampling when either all detection statistics are small, in which case the null hypothesis is selected in all units, or at least one detection statistic is large enough, in which case some non-empty subset of units is identified as the set of signals. Specifically, the proposed test in this case, $\chi^*_{\mathrm{det}}:=(T^*_{\mathrm{det}},D^*_{\mathrm{det}})$, is:
\[
T^*_{\mathrm{det}}:=\min\{T_0,T_{\mathrm{det}}\}\quad\text{and}\quad D^*_{\mathrm{det}}=\emptyset\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T_0<T_{\mathrm{det}},
\]

source_passages.local_label: Section 3.2.3 — The test for joint detection and isolation
source_passages.source_heading: Section 3.2.3 — The test for joint detection and isolation
source_passages.statement_original:
When $\emptyset\in\Psi$ and the goal is to control all four kinds of error, the proposed test in this case, $\chi^*:=(T^*,D^*)$, is based on a combination of the two previous ones:
\[
T^*:=\min\{T_0,T_{\mathrm{joint}}\},\qquad D^*:=\begin{cases}\emptyset&\text{if }T_0<T_{\mathrm{joint}}\\D_{\mathrm{iso}}(T^*)&\text{if }T_{\mathrm{joint}}<T_0,\end{cases}
\]
where $T_0$ is defined as before,
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{\mathrm{joint}}:=\inf\{n\in\mathbb N:{}&\Lambda_{e,\mathrm{det}}(n)\geq D_e\quad\text{for some }e\in\mathcal K,\\
&\Lambda_{e,\mathrm{iso}}(n)\notin(1/A_e,B_e)\quad\text{for every }e\in\mathcal K,\\
&D_{\mathrm{iso}}(n)\in\Psi\setminus\emptyset\},
\end{aligned}
\]
and $\{A_e,B_e,C_e,D_e\}_{e\in\mathcal K}$ are thresholds to be determined so that $\chi^*\in\mathcal C_\Psi(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)$.

source_passages.source_heading: Section 5 — Detection and isolation of anomalous sources
source_passages.statement_original: In this section we apply the results of Sections 2-4 to the problem of detecting and isolating anomalous sources. That is, throughout this section the units are the data sources themselves, i.e., $\mathcal K=\{\{k\}:k\in[K]\}$ and, as a result, the hypotheses refer to the marginal distributions of the data sources. Moreover, we assume that the distributional assumptions (11)-(12) are satisfied, thus, all asymptotic optimality results in Section 4 hold when the subsystems are large enough.

source_passages.statement_original:
To be specific, throughout this section the units are pairs of data sources, i.e.,
\[
\mathcal K=\{\{i,j\}:1\leq i<j\leq K\},
\]
and the components of $X^e$ are independent (resp. dependent) under $P$ when $P^e$ belongs to $\mathcal H^e$ (resp. $\mathcal G^e$) for every $e\in\mathcal K$ and $P\in\mathcal P_\Psi$. We also assume that conditions (11) and (12) are satisfied and, as a result, all asymptotic optimality results in Section 4 hold when the detection and isolation subsystems are equal to $[K]$.

For this result, as well as some others in this section, we also assume that, under any $P\in\mathcal P_\Psi$,
\[
s_1,s_2\subseteq[K]\text{ are disjoint and independent}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\{i,j\}\notin\mathcal A(P)\quad\forall i\in s_1,j\in s_2.
\]
(23)

We also note that, for every $P\in\mathcal P_\Psi$, there is a disjoint partition of $[K]$, $v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_{L(P)}$, such that
\[
P=P^{v_0}\otimes P^{v_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes P^{v_{L(P)}},
\]
where $v_0$ is the subset of $[K]$ that consists of the independent sources under $P$. This decomposition is used in the statement of the main results of this section.
